title: THE FAMILY TREE THEY WOULD HAVE HIDDEN… BUT GOD PUT IT ON THE FIRST PAGE OF THE GOSPEL
paragraphs: THE FAMILY TREE THEY WOULD HAVE HIDDEN… BUT GOD PUT IT ON THE FIRST PAGE OF THE GOSPEL

Before Jesus performed a single miracle, Matthew revealed a family history filled with betrayal, sexual scandal, outsiders, broken marriages, royal failure, and painful consequences. Why would God allow such complicated stories to stand at the entrance to the Gospel? Because the names people might have wanted erased became part of the story announcing the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
There are things about your family you probably don't tell everyone.
Things that happened behind closed doors.

A marriage that fell apart. A father who walked away. A mother who suffered in silence. A betrayal nobody ever apologized for. A relative whose choices left wounds that reached into the next generation.
Maybe there is a chapter of your own life you wish you could tear out.
A decision you cannot undo.
A relationship you regret.
A secret that still makes you uncomfortable when someone mentions the past.
And perhaps, somewhere deep inside, you have wondered whether God looks at your history and sees too much damage to do anything beautiful with it.
Now imagine opening the New Testament for the first time.
You expect thunder. Angels. Miracles. A dramatic announcement that the Savior of the world has arrived.
Instead, Matthew begins with a genealogy.
Names.
Fathers and sons.
Generation after generation.
And tucked inside those names are stories that would make some religious people deeply uncomfortable.
A woman associated with a troubling family deception.
A Canaanite prostitute who believed in Israel's God.
A Moabite widow whose people had a complicated relationship with Israel.
A woman whose husband was killed after a king abused his power.
A royal family marked by idolatry, judgment, and exile.
Matthew doesn't hide them.
He writes them down.
Right there, before the birth of Jesus.
And once you understand why, you may never read Matthew chapter one the same way again.
Because the genealogy of Jesus is not merely a record of where He came from.
It is a declaration of who He came to save.
And there is a difference.
Matthew opens with these words:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ υἱοῦ Δαυὶδ υἱοῦ Ἀβραάμ.”
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou huiou Dauid huiou Abraam.
“This is the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah the son of David, the son of Abraham.” — Matthew 1:1, NIV

The Greek expression βίβλος γενέσεως (biblos geneseōs) can be understood as a record of genealogy or origins. Its wording also recalls the language of the Greek Old Testament, particularly the genealogical formulas in Genesis.
Matthew is doing something deliberate.
He is connecting the arrival of Jesus to the story that began long before Bethlehem.
Jesus is the promised descendant of Abraham, through whom God's blessing would reach the nations (Genesis 12:3; 22:18; Galatians 3:16).
He is the promised Son of David, the rightful King whose kingdom fulfills God's covenant promises (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Luke 1:32–33).
This is not a random collection of ancestors.
It is the unfolding story of God's covenant faithfulness.
But then Matthew makes an unusual choice.
He mentions women.
In an ancient genealogy structured primarily around fathers and sons, their inclusion is striking.
And not just any women.
He names Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
Then, rather than naming Bathsheba directly, he refers to her as “the wife of Uriah.”
Finally, he comes to Mary, the mother of Jesus.
Each inclusion matters.
But not because every woman mentioned was guilty of some notorious sin. That would be an unfair and biblically careless reading.
Some were victims of wrongdoing. Some were outsiders who demonstrated remarkable faith. Some lived through circumstances that exposed the failures of powerful men.
What unites these accounts is not that every woman was scandalous.
It is that God worked through histories human beings could never have arranged into a respectable, uncomplicated family story.
And the first name should make us uncomfortable for reasons far deeper than gossip.
Tamar.
Genesis 38 tells a disturbing story.

Tamar married into Judah's family. Her first husband died. Her second husband also died after acting wickedly. Judah then failed to fulfill his responsibility toward Tamar by withholding his remaining son.
She was left vulnerable, without the security and family future she had been promised.
Eventually, Tamar disguised herself and Judah had sexual relations with her without recognizing who she was.
When her pregnancy became known, Judah was ready to condemn her.
Until the evidence exposed him.
Suddenly, the man prepared to pronounce judgment was confronted with his own wrongdoing.
And Judah said:
“She is more righteous than I.” — Genesis 38:26, ESV
Read that again.
The man who was ready to shame Tamar had to acknowledge his own injustice.
This does not mean every action in the story is presented as a model for believers. It means the narrative exposes Judah's failure and Tamar's mistreatment.
And from that deeply troubled family situation came Perez.
Matthew 1:3 records his name.
Perez became part of the ancestral line leading to David and, ultimately, to Jesus.
Think about that.
God did not approve of Judah's wrongdoing.
God did not call injustice righteousness.
But human failure did not overthrow His redemptive purposes.
There is a truth here for anyone who has suffered because somebody else refused to do what was right.
The injustice committed against you does not give the person who harmed you the authority to define your future.
And for anyone who has behaved like Judah, there is another truth.
Repentance begins when you stop condemning everyone else long enough to acknowledge what you have done.
Some people want the mercy of Jesus while still holding the stones they intended to throw at somebody else.
Judah's story confronts that hypocrisy.
Then Matthew mentions another woman.
Rahab.
And her story begins in a place most people would never associate with the ancestry of the Messiah.
Jericho.
A city facing judgment.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Scripture does not hide that detail (Joshua 2:1; Hebrews 11:31).
But neither does Scripture allow her former occupation to become the final word about her identity.
When Israel's spies entered Jericho, Rahab protected them because she had come to believe that the LORD was the true God.
She declared:
“For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.” — Joshua 2:11, ESV
The Hebrew behind her confession identifies the LORD as יְהוָה (YHWH), God's covenant name, and affirms that He alone is God over heaven and earth.
Rahab was not simply gambling on which army might win.
She was acknowledging the God of Israel.
And Hebrews 11:31 remembers her for faith.
James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of that faith.
The woman who might have been remembered only by her occupation became remembered in Scripture for believing God.
And Matthew 1:5 includes her in the genealogy of Jesus.
Do you see what that means?
Her past was real.
But her past was not her savior, her master, or her final identity.
God's mercy reached into Jericho.
And faith responded.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
You have spent years introducing yourself internally by your worst chapter.
The divorce.
The addiction.
The affair.
The prison sentence.
The years you ran from God.
The things you did when nobody was watching.
You may have repented, but you still punish yourself as though Christ's forgiveness cannot reach that far.
Listen carefully.
The Bible never teaches that sin is harmless.
But it does teach that the grace of Jesus Christ is sufficient to forgive repentant sinners.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, ESV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue living in rebellion.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And Rahab's story reminds us that faith can begin in places religious people might have already written off.
But Matthew is not finished.
Ruth.
Her story is different.
There is no biblical basis for treating Ruth as a sexually immoral woman or assuming she had a scandalous past.
Ruth was a Moabite widow.
She knew grief.
She knew displacement.
She knew what it meant to face an uncertain future.
And she came from a people whose history with Israel included hostility and serious religious tensions.
Yet when Naomi urged her to return to her own people, Ruth refused to abandon her.
She said:
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” — Ruth 1:16, ESV
Those words were not merely sentimental.
They expressed loyalty, belonging, and a remarkable commitment to the God of Israel.
Ruth entered Bethlehem as a vulnerable foreign widow.
Through the providence of God, she married Boaz, became the mother of Obed, and entered the family line of King David.
And Matthew records her name.
A foreign woman.
A widow.
Someone who might have seemed to stand at the margins of Israel's story.
Yet she was included in the ancestry of Israel's Messiah.
The point is not that Ruth had a shameful secret.
The point is that God's covenant purposes were never as narrow as human prejudice.
Long before Jesus commissioned His disciples to make disciples of all nations, the story leading to His birth already included people from beyond Israel.
The Savior born in Bethlehem would ultimately be proclaimed to the world.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be an outsider.
To walk into a room and wonder whether you belong.
To be judged because of your background, your poverty, your nationality, your family name, or something you cannot change.
Ruth's story does not promise that faithfulness will always produce marriage, financial security, or earthly success.
It shows something better.
God sees faithful people whom society may overlook.
And belonging to Him is not determined by whether human beings consider your background impressive.
Then Matthew brings us to a story that is even more painful.
Because this time, the wrongdoing comes from a king.
David. Bathsheba. Uriah.
Matthew 1:6 says that David was the father of Solomon “by the wife of Uriah.”
The Greek reads:
“ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου”
ek tēs tou Ouriou.
Literally, “from the [woman] of Uriah.”
Matthew does not use Bathsheba's name here.
He identifies her through Uriah.
And that wording draws attention to a history that Israel could not honestly celebrate without remembering its moral cost.
Second Samuel 11 tells us that David saw Bathsheba, sent for her, and slept with her.
The text places the initiative and royal power in David's hands. It does not establish that Bathsheba freely consented, and we should not portray her as equally responsible for the king's actions.
When Bathsheba became pregnant, David tried to conceal what had happened.
When his plan failed, he arranged for Uriah, her husband, to be placed in deadly battle conditions.
Uriah died.
David then took Bathsheba as his wife.
And Scripture delivers one of the most devastating sentences in the account:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 11:27, ESV
Not a misunderstanding.
Not a harmless private matter.
Not merely an unfortunate mistake.
Evil.
Committed by a man who had been given tremendous responsibility.
David was Israel's king.
But his position did not place him above God's moral law.
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David confessed, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13).
God forgave David, yet serious consequences followed. Forgiveness did not erase the suffering caused by his actions.
That distinction matters.
Grace does not mean God pretends the harm never happened.
Grace does not require victims to deny their wounds.
Grace does not turn abuse of power into a romantic love story.
And repentance does not entitle a wrongdoer to immediate trust or freedom from accountability.
The God who forgives sinners is also the God who loves righteousness and justice.
Yet Matthew still includes this part of David's family history.
Why?
Because the promise of the Messiah did not depend on David being morally flawless.
It depended on God's faithfulness.
David needed the Savior who would come from his own line.
The king needed a King greater than himself.
And centuries later, Jesus would be called the Son of David.
But unlike David, Jesus would not exploit His authority to take from the vulnerable.
He would lay down His life to save sinners.
David used power and brought death to another man's household.
Jesus willingly surrendered His life to bring salvation to those who believe.
That contrast should make us worship.
Because the greatest King in the story is not the one who sat on David's throne.
It is the One who wore a crown of thorns.
And then comes another astonishing detail.
Matthew does not end his genealogy with David's greatness.
He takes us through generations of kings.
Some faithful.
Some wicked.
Some responsible for leading God's people into devastating spiritual compromise.
Then comes exile.
Matthew 1:11–12 places the Babylonian deportation directly inside the genealogy.
The royal family did not move from uninterrupted triumph to the manger.
It passed through judgment, national catastrophe, and displacement.
The kingdom fell.
Jerusalem suffered.
The people were carried away.
And still, the genealogy continued.
That does not mean the exile was insignificant.
It was a profound consequence of covenant unfaithfulness, as the prophets repeatedly explained.
But God's promises had not vanished.
Even through judgment, He preserved the line through which the Messiah would come.
Some of you understand that kind of waiting.
You have prayed for restoration and watched things grow worse before they got better.
You have watched a family break apart.
You have buried someone you expected to grow old beside.
You have stood in the ruins of decisions you made or decisions made against you.
And you have wondered whether God is still working when the evidence around you looks like loss.
Matthew's genealogy reminds us that the history of redemption included seasons when God's people were not living in visible victory.
The exile was real.
The suffering was real.
And God's faithfulness was real.
But then Matthew reaches a turning point.
After generations of repeating the pattern of fathers and sons, his wording changes.
Matthew 1:16 says:
“Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, and Mary was the mother of Jesus who is called the Messiah.” — NIV
Notice what Matthew does not say.
He does not say Joseph fathered Jesus in the same way the preceding men fathered their sons.
The Greek construction shifts:
“ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη Ἰησοῦς”
ex hēs egennēthē Iēsous.
“From whom Jesus was born.”
The relative pronoun ἧς (hēs) is feminine singular, referring to Mary.
Matthew deliberately distinguishes Jesus' birth from the preceding father-to-son formula.
And immediately afterward, Matthew 1:18–25 explains why.
Mary conceived through the Holy Spirit.
Jesus' birth was miraculous.
Joseph was His legal father, but not His biological father.
The genealogy establishes Jesus' place within the Davidic family through Joseph's legal relationship, while the birth narrative reveals that Jesus' conception was the work of the Holy Spirit.
This is not simply another generation.
This is the arrival of the promised Christ.
And here is where everything changes.
The genealogy is not telling us that Jesus inherited the moral guilt of His ancestors.
He did not.
Scripture teaches that Jesus was without sin (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22).
Nor is Matthew suggesting that God approved of every action recorded in the ancestral narratives.
He did not.
Instead, Matthew shows us that the sinlessness of Christ and the faithfulness of God shine against the backdrop of a deeply imperfect human history.
The family tree contains people who sinned.
People who suffered.
People who believed.
People who failed.
People who were excluded by social expectations.
People who experienced judgment.
And people who received mercy.
Then comes Jesus.
Not another sinner needing redemption.
The Redeemer Himself.
The One who entered human history without becoming morally corrupted by it.
The One who came not to excuse sin, but to save His people from their sins.
Matthew 1:21 makes His mission unmistakable:
“You are to give him the name Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.” — NIV
In the Hebrew and Aramaic-speaking world of Jesus' time, His name corresponds to יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua), related to the Hebrew name Yehoshua, meaning “the LORD saves” or “YHWH is salvation.”
The name fits the mission Matthew announces.
Jesus came to save.
Not merely to improve humanity's reputation.
Not to make broken people appear respectable.
Not to cover wickedness with religious language.
He came to deal with sin at its deepest level.
Through His obedient life, sacrificial death, and resurrection, He accomplishes what no ancestor, king, priest, or ordinary human being could accomplish.
He reconciles sinners to God.
This is why the genealogy matters.
Because before Matthew tells us what Jesus did, he shows us the world into which Jesus came.
A world filled with broken promises.
Unfaithful leaders.
Complicated families.
Grieving widows.
Foreigners seeking refuge.
Guilty people in need of mercy.
And generations waiting for God's salvation.
Does any of that sound familiar?
Maybe you are reading this while everyone else in your house is asleep.
Maybe you are smiling in public while privately carrying guilt you have never confessed.
Maybe you are angry because someone used their authority to hurt you and then demanded that you remain silent.
Maybe your family history is filled with addiction, abandonment, violence, infidelity, or spiritual confusion.
Maybe you grew up believing that people from families like yours do not become strong Christians.
That holiness belongs to other households.
That God uses people with cleaner histories.
But listen to what Matthew is showing you.
Your ancestry does not determine whether the grace of Christ is available to you.
Your family name cannot save you.
And your family name cannot make the cross of Jesus powerless.
You are not saved because your ancestors were righteous.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
You are not made holy by pretending your past never happened.
You are called to bring your sin into the light, repent, believe the Gospel, and walk in newness of life.
And if you were the one harmed by somebody else's sin, the Gospel does not demand that you carry their guilt as though it were yours.
Christ calls us into truth.
Not denial.
Into forgiveness.
Not the celebration of evil.
Into transformation.
Not a performance of perfection.
There is a phrase that captures the heartbeat of this entire genealogy.
But we must understand it correctly.
It does not mean scandal is beautiful.
It does not mean suffering is good.
It does not mean every painful family story will resolve neatly before we die.
It means the God of Scripture is powerful enough to fulfill His righteous purposes in a world where sin has caused terrible damage.
And in Jesus Christ, He offers something greater than the rehabilitation of a family reputation.
He offers redemption.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or gift, depending on context.
And the grace revealed in Christ is not a reward for having a respectable past.
It is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, made known through Jesus.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — NIV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had fixed the family.
Not after we had cleaned up every memory.
Not after we had earned a better name.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is where Matthew's genealogy stops being a passage you rush through and becomes a mirror you cannot easily look away from.
Because somewhere among those names, you may recognize your own need.
Perhaps you recognize Judah's hypocrisy.
Perhaps Rahab's need for mercy.
Perhaps Ruth's longing to belong.
Perhaps the pain of Bathsheba's story.
Perhaps David's need to confess.
Perhaps the despair of exile.
But the most important question is not which person in the genealogy resembles you.
The most important question is what you will do with Jesus.
Because the genealogy leads to Him.
Every promise.
Every generation.
Every surprising name.
Every reminder of human failure.
Every testimony of faith.
All of it brings the reader to the arrival of the Messiah.
And Jesus did not come merely to give us an inspiring family story.
He came to call sinners to repentance and faith.
He came to forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile.
To make people new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: The old has gone, the new is here!” — NIV
That is not a promise that every earthly consequence instantly disappears.
It is a promise of a new identity and life in Christ.
Your past may still require confession.
Restitution where possible.
Accountability.
Healing.
Rebuilding trust.
And patient obedience.
But for those who belong to Jesus, the past no longer has the authority to pronounce God's final verdict.
Christ does.
And His Gospel calls us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
So perhaps tonight, the most important thing you can do is stop running.
Stop defending the sin God is calling you to confess.
Stop believing that your wounds make you unworthy of being loved.
Stop measuring the power of Jesus by the failures of the people who claimed to represent Him.
Look to Christ Himself.
The spotless Lamb of God.
The Son of David.
The Son of Abraham.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One whose earthly family history included broken people, yet whose own life was perfectly holy.
And surrender to Him.
You do not need to invent a beautiful testimony before you come to Jesus.
You need Jesus.
And if this truth has exposed something you have been carrying, I want to invite you into an honest moment.
You do not have to share private details publicly. God knows the things you cannot yet put into words.
Someone who thinks their life is beyond redemption may need to hear that Jesus is still saving and transforming lives.
There is another reason this message deserves to travel beyond this page.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who has quietly decided that their history makes them unacceptable to God.
They may never tell you.
Not simply to increase a page's reach, but because the truth of the Gospel deserves to be heard by people who may never walk into a church on their own.
Return to it when you read Matthew 1 again.
Return to it when your past tries to speak louder than the promises of God.
Return to it when you need to remember that the Bible tells the truth about human sin while pointing us to the greater truth of Christ's saving grace.
Not because a social media page can replace your local church, your pastor, or your personal time in God's Word.
But sound biblical teaching and daily encouragement can help strengthen believers and introduce seekers to the truth of Jesus Christ.
And I want to speak personally for a moment about something important.
Behind every article, every biblical study, every free resource, and every message shared with someone who is struggling, there is ongoing work.
Research.
Writing.
Preparation.
Time.
And the practical cost of continuing and expanding this ministry.
It is a voluntary way of partnering with this ministry so that we can continue producing Christ-centered teaching, developing discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the Gospel.
But I want to be clear about something Scripture makes important.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not the result of pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your responsibilities to your family and your local church should not be neglected.
And the Gospel itself is not for sale.
The free resources remain a genuine expression of our desire to serve.
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation and opportunities to carry encouraging messages into everyday life.
They are not spiritual rewards.
The greatest gift is still the Gospel of Jesus Christ, freely proclaimed.
Pray for those who read it.
Invite a friend to study Matthew chapter one.
Encourage someone who has been hiding from God.
Point someone toward Jesus.
Because the goal is not to build a following around a personality.
It is to help people follow Christ.
And that brings us back to where we started.
A genealogy.
A list of names.
A passage many readers skip because they assume nothing important is happening.
But Matthew knew exactly what he was doing.
He was announcing that the long-awaited Son of Abraham and Son of David had come.
He was showing that God had remained faithful through generations of human weakness, unexpected faith, moral failure, and historical upheaval.
He was preparing us to meet the One whose name means that the Lord saves.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is this:
Jesus did not enter a world that had finally become worthy of Him.
He entered a world that desperately needed Him.
He came into the history of sinners.
But He was not conquered by their sin.
He carried the cross.
He bore our sins.
He rose from the grave.
And He calls us to follow Him.
So when you read Matthew's genealogy again, don't rush past Tamar.
Don't reduce Rahab to her former occupation.
Don't overlook Ruth's faithfulness.
Don't forget Uriah when you read David's name.
Don't treat the exile as a meaningless interruption.
And above all, don't miss Jesus.
Because the genealogy is not ultimately a celebration of complicated ancestors.
It is a testimony to the faithfulness of God and the arrival of the Savior.
Your family history may explain some of the wounds you carry.
Your choices may explain some of the consequences you face.
But neither your ancestry nor your worst failure has the power to make the saving grace of Jesus Christ insufficient.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
And let the One who entered a broken human history begin His transforming work in yours.
The names people might have wanted erased were not the end of the story—because the final name in Matthew's genealogy is Jesus.
